briefing20814.title: In 20814, the county marks 66 of 138 buildings “No.”
briefing20814.description: What Montgomery County’s BEPS inventory and energy performance map show for ZIP 20814 as of November 7, 2026: projected interim standard readings by building type, coverage gaps, and an October permits comparison.
briefing20814.author: Max Fisher
briefing20814.body:
County exports retrieved November 7, 2026 · ZIP {{zip}} · Montgomery County, Maryland · Energy map reporting-year label, as published: {{reporting_year_label}}

The finding. Montgomery County’s energy performance map lists {{interim.no}} of the {{matched}} matched buildings in ZIP {{zip}} as not meeting their projected interim performance standard. {{interim.yes}} read Yes and {{interim.undisclosed}} read Undisclosed. Hotels ({{use.hotel.no}} of {{use.hotel.records}}) and multifamily housing ({{use.multifamily housing.no}} of {{use.multifamily housing.records}}) account for most of the No readings. Offices run the other way: {{use.office.yes}} of {{use.office.records}} read Yes.

What it can inform

The county publishes a projection for each building it tracks. Where one building type sits mostly on the “No” side, that type is where the county’s own figures put the most distance between published energy use and the interim standard. For an HVAC business that serves, or wants to serve, larger buildings in {{zip}}, that makes it the building type to understand first: how those buildings are typically heated and cooled, who makes system decisions, and what the county’s rules ask of them.

The decision it can inform: which building type to study first, and which questions to bring to that conversation. It cannot tell you which building to call.

By building type

Matched records only. Use types from the county inventory; readings from the energy map’s “Meeting Interim Standard” field.

{{TABLE:by_use}}

Against the projected final standard, the split widens: {{final.no}} read No, {{final.yes}} read Yes, and {{final.undisclosed}} read Undisclosed.

How to read the columns

The map carries a “Benchmarking Report Status” column and separate “Meeting Interim Standard” and “Meeting Final Standard” columns. The first tracks whether a building’s benchmarking report was filed and accepted. The standard columns compare the building’s published energy use with its projected targets. {{interim_no_and_report_in_compliance}} of the {{interim.no}} buildings that read No for the interim standard read “in compliance” for benchmarking report status. Read each column on its own terms. Neither one is a compliance determination by MBRACE INSIGHT.

Coverage and gaps

  • {{inventory_in_zip}} inventory records and {{energy_in_zip}} energy map records list postal code {{zip}}. All {{matched}} energy map records matched an inventory record by exact county building ID.
  • {{unmatched_count}} inventory records have no energy map match: two multifamily buildings (named “Cecil” and “Hampden House” in the inventory) and one record with no name or use type.
  • Among matched records, {{eui_blank}} have a blank normalized net site EUI and {{eui_undisclosed}} read “Undisclosed.” Both Undisclosed interim readings are multifamily buildings.
  • ZIP comes from the county’s published postal code. We did not assign ZIPs from street addresses. Two records elsewhere in the export carry invalid postal codes and are outside this scope.
  • The reporting-year label ({{reporting_year_label}}) is the county’s. We have not mapped it to a calendar year of energy use.

What it does not show

Equipment type, age, or condition. An owner’s plans, budget, or timeline. Whether a building qualifies for an exemption or will pursue an alternative pathway. Any project, bid, or purchase. Confirm the building record and the county’s current requirements before relying on any value.

The permits comparison

The county’s Mechanical Permits dataset lists {{permits.county}} permits with October 2026 issue dates; the latest issue date in the data is {{permits.last_issue_date}}, and the source last reported a row update on October 30. {{permits.zip}} list ZIP {{zip}}: {{permits.worktype.REPLACE}} replacements and {{permits.worktype.INSTALL}} installs, covering {{permits.usecode.SINGLE FAMILY DWELLING}} single-family dwellings, {{permits.usecode.TOWNHOUSE}} townhouses, and {{permits.usecode.BUSINESS BUILDING}} business buildings. That is recorded permitting activity, mostly residential, and a different population from the BEPS buildings above. City permit systems are outside the dataset, and a permit does not confirm the equipment type or completed work.

Method

  1. Downloaded the county BEPS building inventory and the energy performance map with their official export controls on November 7, 2026, and recorded each file’s SHA-256 checksum.
  2. Kept records whose published postal code is {{zip}}.
  3. Joined the two exports on exact county building ID. No name-based or fuzzy matching.
  4. Kept every published value as text, including blanks and “Undisclosed,” and counted directly from those values.
  5. Queried the county Mechanical Permits API for October issue dates and confirmed the download matched an independent count query. A recheck on November 7 returned the same {{permits.county}} records.

Sources

  • Montgomery County BEPS building inventory. Export file time {{sources.inventory.file_time_utc}}; SHA-256 {{sources.inventory.sha256}}.
  • Montgomery County energy performance map. Export file time {{sources.energy.file_time_utc}}; SHA-256 {{sources.energy.sha256}}.
  • Montgomery County Mechanical Permits dataset. Retrieved {{sources.permits.retrieved_utc}}.
  • Montgomery County BEPS scope announcement.

Every building-level value is in the 20814 BEPS Data Sheet. Send a correction or a source to mfisher@mbraceinsight.com.

rebates.title: A rebate headline is not an approval.
rebates.description: A source-checked starting point for DMV heat pump rebates, program timing, and tax-credit questions.
rebates.author: Max Fisher
rebates.body:
A national incentive headline is a starting point. Your address, utility, household, equipment, and project timing determine which program rules you need to read. A program cap is not an award for your home.

DC: identify the program route

DOEE directs federally funded home-energy assistance through AHEP and AHRA. It describes DCSEU residential rebates as a separate route. Check the specific program before comparing offers. Read DOEE’s program explanation ↗

Maryland: distinguish a proposed launch from an open application

MEA’s September 30, 2026 update says revised federal rebate applications were submitted and launch depends on DOE approval. This does not establish access to a federal rebate today. Separate utility offers need their own review. Check MEA’s current status ↗

Virginia: use the current FAQ

Virginia Energy’s October 13, 2026 FAQ says its federal Home Energy Rebates are not yet available. Final access procedures and launch timing remain unsettled. Ask about existing alternatives through the agency’s links. Read Virginia Energy’s FAQ ↗

Rebates and tax credits are different

Do not carry old tax-credit copy into a 2026 budget. The IRS describes the Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit for improvements made through December 31, 2025. That is not a promised credit for a new 2026 installation. Check the IRS timing rules ↗

Five checks before a purchase

  1. Confirm your service address and electric utility.
  2. Identify the exact program and its administrator.
  3. Ask whether preapproval, an assessment, or a participating contractor is required.
  4. Get written confirmation of qualifying equipment, timing, documentation, and payment process.
  5. Keep the dated program terms alongside your quote.

These are research steps, not an eligibility determination. Recheck the official program when making a decision; this briefing is a dated snapshot.

beps.title: BEPS starts with the building.
beps.description: How DMV residents and condo owners can start checking building-performance coverage and responsibilities.
beps.author: Max Fisher
beps.body:
Building Energy Performance Standards, or BEPS, concern the performance of covered buildings. Start with the building and jurisdiction, then establish who is responsible for the records. A regional headline cannot establish your home’s obligations.

Maryland and Montgomery County are distinct programs

MDE identifies commercial and multifamily buildings of at least 35,000 square feet for its state program, subject to exemption procedures. Montgomery County describes its local BEPS program as covering most commercial and multifamily buildings of at least 25,000 square feet. These thresholds are a screening step, not a final determination. Maryland program ↗ · County scope and adopted regulation ↗

DC has its own program

DOEE maintains DC’s BEPS program and directs readers to its current building-energy portal. Use that jurisdiction’s records and guidance to establish coverage and applicable requirements. Start with DC DOEE ↗

If you own a condo or rent

Ask the association or building manager which building record applies, whether coverage has been confirmed, who manages benchmarking, and where the current plan and deadlines are recorded. A unit owner’s decisions and whole-building responsibilities can be different.

What a performance gap does not establish

A disclosed energy metric or a gap to a future target does not by itself prove current noncompliance, identify required HVAC work, or establish a project budget. Check reporting status, applicable deadlines, approved pathways, and official correspondence before drawing that conclusion.

A useful next conversation

Bring your building address, jurisdiction, building ID if available, current reporting record, and questions to the program administrator or your qualified adviser. This is an educational starting point, not legal advice, a compliance certification, or an engineering assessment.

planning.title: Look past the heat pump price tag.
planning.description: Questions to ask before comparing heat pump proposals and relying on a potential rebate.
planning.author: Max Fisher
planning.body:
A useful heat pump conversation starts with your home and the scope of work. Keep equipment choices, home conditions, incentives, and installation responsibilities in the same record so you can compare like with like.

Describe the home before comparing prices

Record your current heating and cooling equipment, its age if known, the rooms that are uncomfortable, and the upgrades you are considering. Ask the contractor how the proposal accounts for your home’s heating and cooling needs. Keep model numbers and assumptions in the quote.

Ask what is included

Ask about the assessment, electrical and duct work, controls, permits, removal of old equipment, commissioning, warranty, and service arrangements. Identify exclusions and who is responsible for each step. These questions help define a scope; this worksheet does not size or design your system.

Resolve program requirements before relying on a discount

Some programs require an assessment or a particular contractor process. Virginia’s current FAQ, for example, describes assessment requirements in its proposed federal programs and warns against assuming a project will qualify before launch. Read the program’s own requirements ↗

Use a decision record

For each proposal, write down the cash price, separately identified potential incentive, who applies, what evidence is needed, and whether approval is confirmed or pending. Ask how a funding delay or rejection would affect your payment obligation.

Keep the next step practical

Use the Quote Companion to collect answers. Confirm the program terms with the administrator and technical scope with a qualified contractor before making a commitment. No savings, rebate eligibility, or particular equipment outcome is guaranteed by this guide.

privacy.title: Your email. A clear choice.
privacy.body:
This is a private MBRACE INSIGHT website draft. The site helps DMV residents understand heat pumps, electrification incentives, and building-performance requirements. It records resource requests and newsletter preferences in a private database.

What is recorded

Your email address, request type, requested asset, signup source, supplied campaign tags, timestamp, and the consent wording/version are stored. Historical clearance requests, if submitted through a retained link, also store a public page URL and target query. Do not enter private signed links or credentials. Short-lived hashed request markers help limit abuse; raw network addresses are not stored in the contact list.

Resources and newsletter are separate

Entering your email for a resource records that request and gives you a download link. It does not request the newsletter unless you choose the separate checkbox. Standalone newsletter signup requires an explicit choice. Repeated requests use one contact record while retaining distinct request and consent events.

Confirmation and delivery

Newsletter requests remain pending email confirmation. This private preview does not send confirmation emails or newsletters automatically. An email delivery platform has not yet been connected. Download access is available immediately after a successful saved request.

Your preferences

A private preference link is shown after each successful request. Use it to withdraw newsletter signup or mark the address unsubscribed. Opening that link alone does not change preferences; the form requires a deliberate confirmation. For access, correction, or removal requests, contact mfisher@mbraceinsight.com.

Access and storage

The site uses Sites hosting with a private D1 database. Contact records and exports are restricted to the publisher. Test addresses ending in .invalid are excluded from the real-list exports. The hosting provider may process technical information to deliver and protect the site. External source sites have their own practices.

Before public launch

Final privacy terms, retention rules, the email confirmation/delivery workflow, editorial review, and the actual public page’s six-gate validation require completion. Subscriber data is not part of an unrestricted research or RAG corpus.

editorial.title: The source comes with the story.
editorial.description: Our approach to sources, dated program information, corrections, and independence.
editorial.author: Max Fisher
editorial.body:
MBRACE INSIGHT is an independent publication for HVAC owners and operators in Maryland, starting in Montgomery County. We report what public records show (building energy filings, permits, and other attributable sources) and keep source observations, our calculations, and estimates labeled separately.

What insider insight means here

We read program details, explain the differences between jurisdictions, and connect those details to practical questions. We do not claim privileged government access, official agency status, or access to unannounced funding.

Sources and dates

Time-sensitive statements link to the responsible agency or program. A source-checked date records when we reviewed that information. It is not a promise that the information remains unchanged or that the page updates automatically.

Evidence and interpretation

Program status, quoted rules, and our interpretation are kept distinct. Missing information stays unknown. A program headline does not establish household eligibility; a building’s performance data does not by itself establish noncompliance.

Corrections and responsibility

Max Fisher is the responsible publisher. Send a source, a correction, or a question to mfisher@mbraceinsight.com. Material corrections should identify what changed and when. No government endorsement or installation service is claimed.

Commercial relationships

Any future paid placement, affiliate link, or referral relationship must be clearly identified where it appears. This draft does not present a paid contractor directory or endorse a provider. The separate SEO agency is outside this publication’s resident-facing offer.

Publishing quality

Semantic Gate remains our internal six-gate release requirement for the final public URL and target query. This owner-private draft is not publicly certified. It retains private access and indexing restrictions pending launch review.
